description: We are a passionate group of university students and game makers dedicated to exploring and sharing the wonders of astronomy in every way we can. As developers of a space mission launching game, we love translating real aerospace concepts into engaging, interactive experiences. At the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to combine our game-making creativity with space science to build projects that inspire others to look up.
summary:
Space Con is a browser-based, multiplayer rocket design and space exploration game built for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players build their own rockets from capsules, fuel tanks, engines and stages, and the game recalculates mass, thrust-to-weight ratio, delta-v and cost after every change. Players then launch, pick a target on a solar system map, wait for the right transfer window and fly there. Once they arrive, they set up a colony whose income pays for bigger missions. Up to 16 players can play online at the same time, racing to be the first to reach and claim a planet.

The game’s physics runs on NASA data. Planet radius, gravity and atmosphere come from NASA NSSDC. Orbits and planet positions come from NASA mission-viz and JPL SSD. Rocket performance uses the rocket equation from NASA Glenn.

This matters because rocket science feels abstract to most beginners. In Space Con, a bad design costs a player the mission and money, so they learn thrust, gravity, delta-v and orbits by trying things out instead of memorizing formulas. Learning space mission design becomes hands-on, social and fun.
details:
What it does
Space Con is a browser-based, multiplayer rocket design and space exploration game built for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Every game follows three steps:

  1. Design your rocket. In the assembly screen, players drag and drop capsules, probes, fuel tanks, engines (from chemical to ion and nuclear NERVA) and stage separators onto a grid. After every change the game recalculates the rocket’s mass, thrust-to-weight ratio (TWR), delta-v per stage and in total, and cost. A built-in delta-v guide shows roughly how much a mission needs: about 2,400 m/s to reach orbit, +1,300 m/s for the Moon, +1,100 m/s for Mars or Venus.
  2. Fly and choose your planet. On the solar system map, the planets move along orbits computed from NASA/JPL data, so every target has its own transfer window. The game tells players how big a burn they need and how long until the window opens. Flight readouts show altitude, speed, apoapsis/periapsis and remaining delta-v. Helper commands (go to target, orbit, auto-land, and time warp up to 25×) keep the game accessible.
  3. Claim your planet. Players who reach their target land the modules they carried in their cargo: solar panels, batteries, reactors, habitat domes, space farms, telemetry stations. Together these form a colony that earns regular income, which players spend on bigger rockets and more distant missions.

Up to 16 players can play online at the same time in the same solar system. Each player has their own named launch pad, and the first player to reach a planet and build a base there claims it.

How NASA data is used

  • NASA NSSDC Planetary Fact Sheet: radius, surface gravity and atmosphere, which drive falling, drag, landing and launch.
  • NASA mission-viz and JPL SSD Approximate Positions of the Planets: orbital elements and planet positions, which drive elliptical orbits, current planet positions and transfer windows.
  • NASA Glenn Beginner’s Guide to Aeronautics: specific impulse (Isp), thrust-to-weight and the rocket equation Δv = Isp · g₀ · ln(m₀/m_f), used for the delta-v and lift-off checks in the assembly screen.

We keep source-based values separate from gameplay choices. Some values are scaled for playability: distances, time, engine prices, mission rewards and colony income are game assumptions.

Benefits and intended impact
Rocket physics feels abstract when it’s only formulas. In Space Con, a bad design costs a player the mission and money, so they learn thrust, mass, gravity, delta-v and orbital transfers by trying things out: wrong design → failure → better design → understanding. The game is built for students and anyone curious about space, and needs no advanced engineering knowledge. Multiplayer racing makes learning social and motivating.

Tools and technologies
React, TypeScript and Vite for the web interface; Zustand for game state; Phaser for the 2D scene and flight. We used automated tests for the physics calculations and game logic, plus build checks.

Creativity
Space Con combines a rocket-building sandbox, real NASA/JPL orbital data and a real-time multiplayer race for planets in one browser game. Planet positions follow real orbits, so timing a launch for a transfer window becomes part of the strategy.

Limitations
Space Con is an educational, simplified 2D model (single plane, no rotation, no reentry heating). It is not a mission-planning tool.
